analysis.one_liner: Lets employers who underpaid workers self-audit and repay back wages without penalties.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 14, 2025 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make permanent a Department of Labor program, first piloted in 2018, where employers who inadvertently broke federal minimum wage or overtime rules can run a self-audit, calculate what they owe, and pay workers the full back wages directly under Labor Department supervision. In exchange, workers who accept the settlement give up their right to sue for additional damages, and the employer's audit materials cannot be used against it or discovered in court. Employees can decline the offer and keep their right to sue.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who were underpaid get their back wages faster and with less hassle than a government investigation, if their employer volunteers for the program. Employers who underpaid workers gain a supervised, penalty-free way to settle: they pay what they owe but avoid the extra 'liquidated damages' (an equal amount again) and class-action lawsuits they would otherwise face, and the audit paperwork is shielded from future litigation.

how_it_helps.text: Employers self-audit their pay practices, list affected employees, and pay the full unpaid minimum wages or overtime owed, with the Labor Department verifying the calculations and supervising payment [S2].

In the 2018-2019 pilot this is modeled on, 74 cases returned $4.1 million in back wages to 7,429 workers, with each case reaching about 10 times more employees than a traditional investigation and taking far less staff time [S2].
The bill adds protections against retaliation for workers who accept or decline a settlement offer [S2].

Employers qualify only if they have not been found to violate wage law in the prior 5 years, are not already under investigation or litigation over the practice, and have corrected the violating practice [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who accept a settlement give up their right to sue for double damages under the Fair Labor Standards Act for the covered violations. Plaintiffs' side employment lawyers lose potential cases and fees, since settled violations cannot be relitigated. The Department of Labor gives up penalty leverage over participating employers.

drawbacks.text: The employer sets the scope: the Labor Department is barred from expanding an investigation or settlement beyond the violations the employer itself identified in its application [S2].
If an application is denied, the Department may not tell the affected employees about the violations or notify them of their right to sue, so workers may never learn they were shortchanged [S2].

Settlement pays back wages only, with no liquidated damages, and any information submitted is exempt from discovery in court without the employer's consent, which critics of the original pilot said makes underpayment cheaper than compliance [S2].
Workers can decline and keep their right to sue, but many may accept quickly rather than pursue a lengthy lawsuit [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades enforcement teeth for speed and reach. Workers who might never see a cent through a slow, selective investigation get paid directly, and the pilot data shows the self-audit route recovered far more per staff hour. The cost falls on the same workers: accepting means no double damages, employers control what gets disclosed, and the Department is limited in what it can tell employees or pursue beyond the employer's own audit. Whether that trade favors workers depends on how honestly employers self-report, which is why the program's guardrails matter as much as its payments.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-July 2025 and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, and nothing has happened since, so the outcome is still open.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Sheehy introduced the bill on July 14, 2025, joined by Sens. Marsha Blackburn and Ted Budd [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S4].
No hearing, markup, or floor action has been recorded since referral, and the 119th Congress remains in session [S4].

The bill is one of several reintroductions of a proposal to codify the Labor Department's 2018 Payroll Audit Independent Determination pilot program, which the bill's findings credit with returning back wages more efficiently than traditional enforcement [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far nobody: workers keep their existing right to sue for double damages, and employers get no new self-audit route. The bill's Senate backers have nothing to show for it yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: no one, so far

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no Democrats have signed on; support so far is three Republican senators, so the partisan shape is unknown.

industries.note: The bill gives underpaying employers a supervised way to repay back wages while escaping liquidated damages and lawsuits, with the audit paperwork shielded from discovery and the government barred from investigating beyond what the employer discloses. Workers get paid, but employers' cost of having underpaid drops below what current law allows workers to recover.

Settled violations are waived by workers who accept, and self-audit materials cannot be used in court, shrinking the pool of cases and fees. Their interest in maximum recovery for workers runs alongside workers' own full legal remedies.

Participating employers must pay full back wages verified by the Labor Department, and the pilot reached far more employees per case than traditional investigations. The offset is the waiver of double damages on accepting.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in the HELP Committee for months with no action beyond referral. A one-committee referral with no hearing and no Democratic cosponsors usually means the bill dies when the Congress ends in January 2027; a committee markup would be the first sign of movement.
